articles.title: Watch: NASA’s pencil-thin X-59 supersonic jet spotted flying across US skies
articles.summary: NASA’s pencil-thin X-59 experimental supersonic jet was captured flying over the United States on Wednesday, exactly one year after its maiden flight, as
articles.body: NASA’s pencil-thin X-59 experimental supersonic jet was captured flying over the United States on Wednesday, exactly one year after its maiden flight, as the aircraft began a cross-country journey from California to Florida.Videos of the distinctive aircraft have since surfaced on social media, drawing attention to the milestone. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman responded to one such video on X, writing: “Great catch... X-59 making her way to @NASAKennedy”.The aircraft was en route to NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida when it was spotted by people across the US. Videos of the unusual-looking jet were subsequently widely shared on X, drawing attention to its distinctive pencil-thin design. Its journey comes as the space agency marks a year of flight testing for the experimental aircraft, which is the centrepiece of its Quesst mission.The aircraft traveled escorted by an F-15, an F/A-18 and a Gulfstream C-20.NASA Aeronautics also marked the anniversary in a post on X, saying, “One year. New heights. Faster speeds. Since its first flight on Oct. 28, 2025, NASA's X-59 has continued pushing the boundaries of aviation. See how far we've come in just one year!”The agency shared a comparison of the aircraft’s performance on its first flight and one year later. On October 28, 2025, the X-59 reached an altitude of 12,000 feet, clocked a speed of 230 mph and remained airborne for 67 minutes. It had completed just one flight at the time.By October 28, 2026, the aircraft had reached a maximum altitude of 56,000 feet and a top speed of Mach 1.53. Its longest flight lasted 102 minutes, while its flight count had risen to 41, according to the figures shared by NASA Aeronautics.What makes NASA’s X-59 different?According to NASA, the X-59 is 99.7 feet long and 29.5 feet wide. Its most striking feature is its exceptionally long, narrow nose, which accounts for almost a third of the aircraft’s length. The shape is designed to distribute the shock waves generated during supersonic flight, preventing them from merging into the loud sonic boom commonly heard on the ground.The aircraft is powered by a single engine mounted on top of its fuselage. NASA says this positioning directs engine noise upwards, while the aircraft’s smooth underside helps prevent shock waves from combining.The cockpit is positioned almost halfway along the aircraft and has no conventional forward-facing window. Instead, pilots use NASA’s external vision system, which combines cameras and high-resolution displays to provide a view ahead and below the aircraft.NASA designed the X-59 to fly at Mach 1.4, or approximately 925 mph, at an altitude of 55,000 feet. It is an experimental research aircraft, not a prototype passenger plane, and will never carry passengers.NASA said the X-59’s first flight, piloted by test pilot Nils Larson, took place from the Lockheed Martin Skunk Works assembly site in Palmdale, California, to the agency’s Armstrong Flight Research Center. The initial flight focused on low-speed and low-altitude systems checks.The aircraft is not a prototype for a passenger airliner and will not carry passengers. NASA plans to use it to gather data on the sound generated during supersonic flight and residents’ responses when it flies over selected US communities.NASA said the programme will now move towards acoustic validation, studying the sound produced by the aircraft. The findings are expected to help regulators assess noise standards and the possibility of allowing commercial supersonic flights over land.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Mumbai local train megablock today: Central Railway to suspend Trans-Harbour services, block slow lines between CSMT and Vidyavihar; check timings and routes
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Central Railway's (CR) Mumbai division will operate a megablock today, which could inconvenience commuters.
articles.body: MUMBAI: Central Railway's (CR) Mumbai division will operate a megablock today, which could inconvenience commuters. The block is being carried out for essential engineering and maintenance work on the CR Main Line and Trans-Harbour suburban sections.On the Main Line, a block will be in place between CSMT and Vidyavihar on the UP and DOWN slow lines from 10.55 am to 3.55 pm.On the Trans-Harbour Line, services between Thane and Vashi/Nerul/Panvel will remain suspended from 11.10 am to 4.10 pm.Harbour Line services between CSMT-Goregaon and CSMT-Panvel, as well as Port Line trains between Nerul/Belapur and Uran, will operate as per the standard Sunday schedule.Central Railway has requested commuters to bear with the administration during the inconvenience.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Mumbai | Silver Rate in Mumbai | Bank Holidays in Mumbai | Public Holidays in Mumbai | Mumbai AQI | Weather in Mumbai | Petrol Price in Mumbai | Diesel Price in Mumbai | CNG Price in Mumbai | LPG Price in MumbaiStay updated with the latest Mumbai news. articles.title: Woman rescues an injured queen bumblebee, helps her recover and creates a sheltered space for her; 100 days later, Phoebee has become an online sensation
articles.summary: We hear rescue stories every day. A dog pulled from a flooded ditch. A cat coaxed out from behind a fridge.
articles.body: We hear rescue stories every day. A dog pulled from a flooded ditch. A cat coaxed out from behind a fridge. But how often have you heard about a bumblebee with a broken wing?Gilly McArthur found one lying in the sun beside a road. She took it home, made it a bed of flowers and expected it wouldn’t last the day. Instead, the bumblebee now climbs McArthur’s arm, works her way around the back of her neck and disappears into her hair. The woman named the queen bee ‘Phoebee’, and strangers from around the world are obsessed with her.“I couldn’t leave her by the roadside. So I brought her home and made her a bed of flowers. I thought she’d be dead in a day or so,” McArthur told The Guardian, describing the extraordinary rescue. Contrary to McArthur’s fears, Phoebee survived and also became an internet celebrity.An unexpected travel partnerMcArthur was due to leave on a week-long sailing trip shortly after the rescue. She couldn’t leave the bee behind, so she brought Phoebee along. The woman posted about their voyage together on Instagram. "Phoebee is now at sea. It’s been nearly a month since I found her struggling on a hot concrete pavement in my town, unable to fly because one of her wings had been lost; well, it's now a postcard from us on the West Coast of Scotland. When I picked her I hadn't expected her to last this long!" she wrote on Instagram in August.The next morning, McArthur woke to messages from around the world. People wrote about bumblebees they had rescued, butterflies they had nursed and small creatures they had tried to save. The stories kept flooding in.McArthur is moved by the response but still a little puzzled by it. “I think it might be because the world is in such a polycrisis at the moment, and everyone is wanting to pull back to something authentic and kind,” she told the newspaper. “Perhaps Phoebee reminds people of a time when bumblebees were more prolific, in a world that isn’t on fire: lots of the messages said the videos helped them feel more grounded in a world where the algorithms are usually so grounded in clickbait and violence.”100 days of PhoebeeOn 24 October, McArthur posted a collage video of Phoebee, celebrating 100 days since the rescue. She also shared how the experience had been ‘weird’ yet eventful. “Sure, it's a bit weird, but in this world that we seem to be racing through and destroying at great speed, these small interactions of wonder, and truly observing something tiny and perfectly designed for life, can pack a lot of punch.”McArthur also spoke about her familiarity with bumblebees. “I've a bit of history with bumblebees, rescuing them on swims, popping them onto my head for an easy swim back to shore, so it probably wasn't too surprising that in the end, one would find me, or me it, for this sort of slice of life. Too much to say in a post about this and the wider observations that the bee is teaching me, so I'd better keep writing and see where it lands!” she wrote on Instagram.Over these days, McArthur also observed some of Phoebee’s unique traits. “She’s fascinating: she spends a lot of time cleaning herself like a cat. And I could watch her putting her long tongue out and getting the nectar out of the flowers for hours.”Britain has 24 species of bumblebee and more than 240 species of solitary bee. Most bumblebees live for only a year. Newly mated queens are the exception, hibernating in autumn and emerging in spring to start colonies of their own. Phoebee has not mated, so her future is uncertain.Andy Benson, of the Bumblebee Conservation Trust, is equally bemused by Phoebee. In his view, Phoebee had some natural advantages. She is a buff-tailed bumblebee, one of the biggest and fluffiest of the British species, and she is a queen, which he described as “the biggest and fluffiest of them all”. He praised McArthur’s compassion. “A third of British wild bees and hoverflies are in decline and a quarter of European species are at risk of extinction because of the loss of their natural habitat, climate change and bee-killing pesticides,” he says.The stakes are practical as well as ecological. Pollinators help produce roughly one in three mouthfuls of food, and crops that rely on them, including apples, beans, squashes and almonds, are worth far more than those that do not.Benson suggests giving such bees a home, not in your home, but in your garden. Plant a few flowers in a garden, a balcony box or a patch of earth, and hundreds of bees can find something to eat. Nobody needs to bring one home.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
